id: Dream Ending in a Host of Angels Zipping Me into My Grandmother’s Dress

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Once & could-be-future girl, believe we’re not like you. Sure, the pickup was tucked in dusk, shed all carefree w/ its sunburn shimmer. Still nothing new to say about the creek, how reeds get moony, or when we saw pelicans hold hands & gossip. But y’all must wanna get this close to soft, so here goes: spool heels, silver sleeves w/ pink accents, kind to stifle the trailer static, same color Dot says Granny passed in. Past since good & we did keep her pearls for you, kissed the hems holy, darned the moth marks back to true. Goes: none of it imitation. Goes: we are her barefoot bloodline, butter in the salt pan. Trust you’re not from this sweat but still a goodness. You once most only boy in the yard, laugh into your born polish. Step-joy, uncousin: home is a name you bless in silk & cinch. Believe we’re all alive here. Come hum this lace blood-warm. Glisten.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Once, Sure, Still

outputs.L1:
Once-&-could-be-future girl, believe us: we’re not like you. Sure, the pickup was tucked into dusk, shed of all care, with its sunburn shimmer. Still, there’s nothing new to say about the creek—how the reeds turn moony, or how we once saw pelicans hold hands & gossip. But y’all must want to get this close to soft, so here goes: spool heels, silver sleeves with pink accents, kind enough to stifle the trailer static—the same color Dot says Granny passed in.

Passed since good, & we kept her pearls for you, kissed the hems holy, darned the moth marks back to true. Goes: none of it is imitation. Goes: we are her barefoot bloodline, butter in the salt pan. Trust that you’re not from this sweat but are still a goodness. You, once mostly the only boy in the yard, laugh into your born polish.

Step-joy, uncousin: home is a name you bless in silk & cinch. Believe us—we’re all alive here. Come hum this lace blood-warm. Glisten.
outputs.L2:
Girl you once were and may become again, know this: we are different from you. Yes, at sundown the pickup sat hidden away, easy and unburdened, glowing like sun-reddened skin. There is no fresh way to describe the creek, the reeds turning lunar, or the pelicans we watched clasping hands and trading secrets. Yet y’all must want to come this near to tenderness, so listen: spool-shaped heels, silver sleeves touched with pink—the shade gentle enough to hush the trailer’s static, the same color Dot says Granny wore when she died. She has been gone a good while. We saved her pearls for you, made the hems sacred with our kisses, and mended every moth-eaten place until it was whole again.

Understand: nothing here is counterfeit. We are Granny’s shoeless descendants, richness melting in a pan of salt. You may not come from this sweat, but there is goodness in you still. Once, you were nearly always the only boy in the yard; now laugh inside the shine you were born with. Walk gladly, no-longer-cousin: home is a name you honor with silk and a tightened waist. Trust that every one of us is living here. Come, hum against this lace, warmed by blood. Shine.
outputs.L3:
The speaker insists that their rural family and way of life possess a distinct and deeply rooted authenticity. This identity is grounded not only in ancestry but also in the textures and rhythms of everyday life. Images of dusk settling over the creek, reeds moving near the water, pelicans gathering, and a pickup parked nearby create a familiar landscape shaped by tenderness and intimacy. The natural world and ordinary rural objects become part of the family’s emotional history.

Material possessions also serve as vessels of memory. Clothing, pearls, and garments repaired with care preserve Granny’s presence and honor the inheritance she has passed down. These objects are more than decorative or practical: they connect generations and allow love, skill, and tradition to remain alive in the present.

Within this setting, the addressee—once perceived as a boy—is warmly welcomed and affirmed in a joyful feminine identity. Silk, lace, pearls, and other forms of adornment express transformation not as a rejection of family history, but as a beautiful continuation of it. The family’s inherited objects become tools of recognition and celebration, helping the addressee inhabit a truer sense of self.

Home, therefore, is presented as a living and loving space rather than merely a physical place. It holds the presence of ancestors while making room for change. In this home, memory and transformation coexist, and belonging is expressed through acceptance, care, and celebration.
outputs.L4:
The poem addresses a gender-nonconforming relative with tenderness, using lush rural imagery, inherited clothing, and intimate family memories to explore identity, lineage, and belonging. The natural landscape becomes more than a setting: fields, plants, weather, and familiar places reflect the relative’s growth and transformation. Clothing passed down through the family similarly connects personal self-expression to earlier generations, suggesting that becoming oneself does not require abandoning one’s roots.

Through these images, the speaker presents identity as both deeply personal and inseparable from family history. Memories of relatives and home create a sense of continuity, showing that the addressed person remains part of the family even as they change how they live or present themselves. Their transformation is not portrayed as artificial, disruptive, or foreign. Instead, it is authentic—another form of growth, as natural as the changing countryside—and is sustained by the love of those who came before.

Ultimately, the poem rejects the idea that gender nonconformity must lead to exile or estrangement. Home and family become sources of recognition rather than judgment, while ancestry offers affirmation instead of restriction. By placing the relative within a landscape of shared memory and inherited love, the speaker assures them that they belong: their identity is genuine, their transformation is worthy of celebration, and their place within the family remains secure.
outputs.L5:
**Once, Sure, Still**

Once, I believed every road had a clear destination. I was sure that time would answer every question and heal every wound. Years have passed, and I understand now that life offers few certainties.

Still, I keep moving forward—not because I know where the road leads, but because hope remains. Sometimes, that is enough.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem welcoming a trans woman back to her rural Southern family, blending queer identity, inherited clothing, grandmotherly memory, and tender country imagery. Use ampersands, fragments, and experimental diction.
counterfactuals.output:
Come on in, girl. The screen door still knows your hand—  
its loose-hinged hymn, its clap & shiver.

We kept your grandmother’s blue dress in the cedar chest,  
among mothballs, quilt scraps, a paper sack of buttons.  
Small moons. Milk-teeth. Things waiting  
to become fastenings.

She wore it to church in August,  
when the heat lay down over the pews like a hound  
& the choir rose, damp-browed, hallelujahing.  
Now the hem finds your knees.  
Now her careful stitches learn the grammar of your body—  
daughterward. Homeward. Yes.

Outside, the soybean fields green themselves to dusk.  
Tree frogs tuning their little wet fiddles.  
A jar of lightning bugs on the porch rail,  
each one striking a match for your name.

We may have spoken it late.  
We speak it now.

Honey, beloved, look—  
the tomatoes have split from too much rain,  
the creek keeps carrying every fallen thing  
without asking what it used to be.

Your aunt sets out biscuits & blackberry jam.  
Your father, quiet as fencepost, brings another chair.  
Someone says you have your grandmother’s hands.  
Someone begins to cry into the sweet tea.  
Not sorrow. Not exactly.  
A thawing. A field after frost.

Come in wearing the blue dress  
or denim, or sequins, or nothing inherited  
but your own bright pulse.

Come in with your womanhood—wildflowered, hard-won,  
a little red clay at the heel.  
Come in, child of these pines & storms,  
you who remade the road by walking it.

The whip-poor-will calls from the dark pasture.  
The porch light gathers its gold around you.

& every old house-board, every cicada husk,  
every star hung low over the pasture says:

We see you.

We have room.

Supper’s warm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an intimate, surreal letter from country cousins to a formerly male-presenting relative who returns home in feminine dress. Make the voice loving and affirming, with references to a pickup at dusk, a creek, pelicans, pearls, lace, and a deceased granny.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Cousin,

We saw you first at dusk, stepping down from the pickup where the road gives up and the pasture begins. The sky was bruised purple, and your dress caught the last light as if evening had been saving it for you. Pearls at your throat, lace at your wrists—you looked both newly arrived and long remembered.

We didn’t ask where the old version of you had gone. We knew she had carried you as far as she could.

Come down to the creek with us. The water still slips over the same green stones, though last night three pelicans stood in the shallows, white as dropped handkerchiefs, solemn as preachers. When you passed, they opened their wings. We swear it. Even the minnows flashed like tiny mirrors, eager to show you your true face.

Granny would have understood. She always said the soul was a wild thing, and the body only its Sunday clothes. We can almost hear her now, rattling the screen door, telling us not to stare and then staring hardest herself—proud, curious, full of that fierce old love. She would have touched your pearls and said, *Honey, those were waiting for you.*

So come home. Sit between us on the porch swing. Let the lace gather softly in your lap. We’ll shell peas, drink something sweet, and call you by the name that makes your eyes lift.

You are not a stranger here. You are our cousin, our girl, our kin. The creek knows you. The pelicans know you. Granny knows you.

And we have always loved you—only now we get to love you in the light.

Your country cousins,  
Always
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary Southern Gothic prose poem about gender transition, ancestry, and belonging. Use compressed syntax, invented compound words, colloquial phrases like “y’all,” and vivid images of silk, salt, sweat, trailers, and moonlit reeds.
counterfactuals.output:
By July I had shed my deadname like snakeskin snagged beneath the trailer steps, thin as old silk, shining where the ants carried off its letters. Y’all know how the South keeps everything: jam jars, grudges, baby teeth, the sweatprint of a body before it learns itself. My grandmother’s mirror, foxed black at the edges, held me half-daughter, half-ghost, all becoming. Behind the glass, the ancestors leaned close—cottonmouth-quiet, salt-eyed—counting my bones as if deciding whether I belonged to them or to the moon.

At dusk I walked beyond the rusted trailers, through reeds silvered and whisperbusy. Frogs throbbed in the ditchwater. My shirt clung, sweat-sweet; my new name moved beneath it, a small warm animal. Lord, I was afraid. Lord, I was beautiful. The creek spoke in mudtongue: child, every body is a crossing. I washed my face in that black water and tasted salt—mine, theirs, the whole bloodweather of us.

Come morning, Mama found me sewing moonlit silk into the hem of my Sunday dress. She said nothing, just threaded the needle when my hands shook. Outside, the family graves sweated dew; inside, the trailer walls breathed heat and hymnsmoke. Y’all, belonging ain’t a gate. It’s a porchlight left burning through stormseason. It’s the dead making room. It’s my grandmother’s mirror giving back, at last, not a stranger, not a sin, but kin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine rural relatives addressing their “once & could-be-future girl” cousin and reassuring her that she remains part of the family’s matrilineal bloodline. Write in a lush, fragmented, queer-poetic style and end with a single-word invitation to shine.
counterfactuals.output:
Cousin, honey—come in from that long weather.

We knew you before the world put fences round your name. Knew you in creekwater, in blackberry stain, in the silver underside of leaves. Once-girl, could-be-girl, neither, both—whatever wildflower grammar your spirit chooses.

You are still of us.

Your blood remembers the women: great-aunt hands shelling peas at dusk, grandmother’s red thread, mothers and almost-mothers humming storms out of the kitchen. The line is not a leash. It is a river. It bends for you, bears you, calls you kin.

No courthouse, no church tongue, no hard-eyed town can unmake what the marrow knows.

Come sit. Let us braid your becoming into ours.

Shine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem in the collective voice of a family welcoming a transfeminine loved one home. Contrast farmyard roughness with glamorous inherited garments, treat femininity as an authentic ancestral inheritance rather than imitation, and keep the tone strange, devotional, and tender.
counterfactuals.output:
**HOME LITURGY WITH MUD & SEQUINS**

We have left the gate unlatched for you,  
its iron mouth chewing the wind.

Come in, daughter—  
the hens have scattered their small brown rumors,  
the tractor kneels in its oil,  
and every fencepost wears  
a splintered halo.

We are waiting in our work hands:  
knuckles of weather,  
nails dark with the root-cellar earth,  
palms made blunt by buckets and birth.

Still, we have opened the cedar chest.

See—

your great-grandmother’s foxed satin,  
moon-pale, smelling of cloves;  
the aunties’ rhinestone combs  
flashing like ice in the horse trough;  
a black velvet dress with a waist  
patient as an hourglass;  
pearls gone warm as milk  
against the throat.

None of this is costume.

We say it together  
so the rafters learn:

**none of this is borrowed.**

The silk knew your name  
before we did.  
The hem kept your measure  
through winters of mice and silence.  
Every woman before you  
left one bright door unlocked—  
a clasp, a pleat, a scarlet lining—  
and now you enter through them  
without disguise.

We button you into the family weather.

Outside, the ram strikes the gate.  
The barn drags its rusted shadow.  
Mud worries the ankles  
of your impossible shoes.

Beautiful, we say,  
and mean the shoes,  
the mud,  
your shy hands lifting the skirt,  
the whole rough kingdom  
making room.

Come home.

We have set the table  
with chipped plates and wedding silver.  
We have slaughtered no calf,  
only the old grammar.

Tonight the cows breathe incense.  
Tonight the pitchforks glitter.  
Tonight we braid your hair  
with ribbons saved from funerals,  
because grief, too, must be taught  
a more radiant use.

And when you turn before the mirror,  
we do not call it transformation.

We call it recognition.

We call it the ancestors  
leaning close through the glass,  
their powdered throats, their field-bent backs,  
their lipstick mouths opening with ours:

There you are.  
There you are.  
There you have always been.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
